paragraphs: It is usually said that people gain and collect goods in order to consume them. The owner may consume them directly, or his household may do so. In theory, the household is treated as part of the owner. At least, this is seen as the proper economic goal of getting goods, and the only goal that the theory needs to consider. Such consumption may serve the consumer's physical needs, such as his comfort. It may also serve his so-called higher needs, which are spiritual, artistic or intellectual. Spending goods serves these higher needs in an indirect way, as economic readers know well.

However, consumption is the reason for collecting wealth only if we give the word a meaning very far from its ordinary one. The real motive behind ownership is the wish to do better than others. This wish to compete created ownership, and it stays active as ownership develops. It also shapes every part of society that ownership touches. Owning wealth brings honour, because it sets a person above others. Nothing equally strong can be said for consumption. The same is true of any other reason for getting goods, and above all for collecting wealth.

Of course, we must not forget another fact. In a society where almost all goods are private property, people need to earn a living. For its poorer members, this is a strong reason that never goes away. Some classes usually do manual work and have an unsafe life. They own little and usually save little. For them, the need to survive and to live more comfortably may be the main motive for a time. But we will see later that even among these poor classes, physical need is not as dominant as people have sometimes thought.

On the other hand, consider the members of society who are mainly busy collecting wealth. For them, the need to survive or to be comfortable never plays an important part. Ownership began and grew for reasons that had nothing to do with the minimum needed to live. From the start, the main motive was the honour that wealth gives, which sets the owner apart. Apart from short periods and rare cases, no other motive has taken first place since then.

Property started as booty, which means goods taken in a successful attack and kept as trophies. As long as the group lived close to other hostile groups, owned things or people were useful mainly in one way. They showed that their owner was better than the enemy who had lost them. The habit of separating the interests of a person from those of his group probably came later. Comparison between the owner of the booty and his less successful neighbours in the group surely existed early on. It added to the value of the things owned, but at first it was not the main part of that value. A man's courage was still mainly the courage of his group. The owner of the booty saw himself mainly as the keeper of his group's honour. This shared view of brave acts is also found in later societies, especially when it comes to the honours of war.
